headline: Plastic was made to last. Most of it still is.
dek: In 1907 Leo Baekeland made the first fully synthetic plastic.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: Bugs can't keep up
slides.text: The United States was wiring itself for electricity, and a common natural insulator was shellac, made by lac insects in Asia. Supply was limited. Leo Baekeland, a chemist, set out to make a substitute in the lab.
slides.alt: Two piles of amber and dark red shellac flakes on white paper

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: Heat, pressure, Bakelite
slides.text: In 1907 he combined phenol and formaldehyde under controlled heat and pressure and got Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic. He announced it in 1909. It soon went into car parts, radios and telephones.
slides.alt: A round brown Bakelite radio with a curved station dial, a cloth speaker grille and three knobs
slides.credit: Radio with a Bakelite case, designed by Wells Coates, 1932. Daderot. CC0.

slides.label: Wait, what?
slides.title: Heat can't touch it
slides.text: Once Bakelite set, heat could not melt it and solvents could not dissolve it. That was the selling point: a part that resisted heat and carried no current would keep its shape for good.

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: Made to last, so it does
slides.statLabel: of the 6.3 billion metric tons of plastic waste made by 2015 sat in landfills or the environment, one study estimates
slides.text: Bakelite was first. Most of the plastics that came after it don't biodegrade in any meaningful sense, one of that study's authors says. A 2022 study found plastic particles in the blood of 17 of 22 donors.
also: Source: Geyer, Jambeck and Law, Science Advances, 2017
slides.alt: Plastic bottles, crates, rope, a tire and other debris heaped along a beach, with surf and a mountain behind
slides.credit: Plastic debris in Kanapou Bay, Kaho'olawe, Hawaii, 2012. NOAA. Public domain.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: Not in his lifetime
slides.text: In 1950, six years after Baekeland died, the world made about 2 million metric tons of plastic a year. Plastic in the ocean was first noticed in the 1960s, and scientists named microplastics in 2004. Nothing in 1907 pointed here.

slides.label: The long cleanup
slides.title: Still negotiating
slides.text: In 2022, 175 nations agreed at the UN to write a binding treaty to end plastic pollution, aiming for a draft by the end of 2024. Talks in 2024 and again in 2025 ended without a deal. In 2026 negotiators chose a new chair to try again.

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: Insulation for a country going electric, without waiting on lac insects
Molded parts for cars, radios and telephones, made quickly and cheaply
A material the world was making at about 400 million metric tons a year by 2015
costs: 79% of 6.3 billion metric tons of plastic waste in landfills or the environment by 2015 (Science Advances, 2017)
Plastic particles in the blood of 17 of 22 donors in one 2022 study
A treaty to end plastic pollution, still unwritten after four years of talks
slides.text: Bakelite solved a real shortage. The bill for the age it opened came due long after its inventor died. You decide if it was worth it.

slides.label: Credit for trying
slides.title: We owe him one
slides.text: Baekeland went after a real supply problem in a country running on new electricity, and solved it with chemistry. The waste came from scale and decades he never saw. Asking where a material goes after its job is a question his age taught us.

slides.label: Pattern
slides.title: Too stable to go away
slides.why: Backfires repeat. We sort every one into nine patterns, so you can spot one before you make one yourself.

slides.label: How the pattern works
slides.title: The feature is the flaw
slides.text: Bakelite was prized because it would not break down. Much of what came after shares that toughness. The quality that keeps a part working in a radio for decades keeps a bottle cap intact on a beach for decades.

slides.label: How you do this
slides.title: You build things to last too
slides.text: You glue a shelf to the wall instead of screwing it in, so it never wobbles. It never does. Then you move out, and the shelf won't come off without taking the wall with it.
also: Permanent marker on the shared whiteboard
A temporary workaround still running five years later

slides.label: Lessons
slides.title: What we take from it
items: How long a thing lasts and how long it stays useful are different numbers.
A harm can wait for scale: one factory's output looks nothing like a planet's.
